newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS-Ailing Thai property awaits correction.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ailing Thai property awaits correction.

text.p: Thailand's troubled property market is eerily quiet as developers maintain high prices, and buyers await a long overdue price correction before making their move, property executives said on Tuesday.
"It's all rather scary at the moment... Things are very, very slow," said Philip Finch, research manager at property firm Richard Ellis.

"There are no transactions because people are waiting for the prices to fall. Meanwhile the developers are getting artificial aid from the government so they do not have to lower their prices," said Philip Sheridan, a property analyst at Thaimex Finance and Securities Plc.

With a much needed 200-300 basis points cut in interest rates to stimulate the market highly unlikely following recent attacks on the currency, lower prices are most likely to trigger any short term stimulus, executives said.

But pledges of support from a government desperate to protect a fragile financial system carrying about 800 billion baht ($32 billion) in property loans exposure is encouraging developers to hang on, executives said.
That support includes a cheap mortgage scheme launched last week aimed at first time buyers.

Two government banks offering small mortgages at between nine and 10 percent have been inundated with loan applications from would-be house buyers since the scheme was launched last week, the banks said.

With only 17.5 billion baht available to borrowers, the positive impact will be limited with estimated absorption put at 12,000-20,000 units in a market believed to contain about 300,000 empty units, analysts said.
Developers are also hanging on for proposed state bond funded bailout of troubled projects to get under way.

"The local developers are hanging really tough, and though I've seen plenty of Singaporeans here looking for property and offering to buy at 30-40 percent below cost the locals are just not interested at the moment," said a senior property consultant at a foreign firm.
A further incentive for developers to maintain prices was the limited recourse financiers have to defaulting developers collateral, analysts said.
Even if faced with severe liquidity problems developers can default on interest payments without fearing projects will be repossessed by frustrated financiers, executives said.
Since the start of the year developers Somprasong Land, Natural Park Plc and Sahavirya City Co Ltd have all defaulted on debt obligations.
"Banks and finance houses don't actually have that much real power to force developers to sell at lower prices," said Finch.
"In recalling bad debts. No bank wants to repossess an illiquid asset which they can't sell on... Repossession is a very time consuming (legal) process which can take up to five years," he added.
But a correction was coming, said executives who believe that the government's best efforts will fail to prevent prices falling by around 10 percent this year.
"We are still sticking to our forecast of a fall in capital values of around 10 percent this year or even a bit more," said Finch. ($1 = 25 baht)
